question: How does Raymond James's affiliation-choice model work commercially?

claims.text: The FY2025 10-K (period 2025-09-30, published 2025-11-25) states that Raymond James offers multiple affiliation options, which it calls AdvisorChoice®. Financial advisors primarily affiliate directly as employees or independent contractors, or as employees of third-party RIAs and broker-dealers that the firm serves through its RIA and Custody Services (RCS) division.

The 2025 10-K describes employee advisors as working in a traditional branch supported by local management and administrative staff, serving predominantly retail clients. Independent contractor advisors are generally responsible for all their direct costs. They may affiliate directly or through an affiliated bank or credit union in the Financial Institutions Division. The 10-K says the independent contractor options are designed to let advisors use as much or as little of the firm's support as they determine they need.

The 2025 10-K reports 8,943 advisors as of September 30, 2025: 3,878 employees and 5,065 independent contractors. The prior-year figures were 3,826 employees and 4,961 independent contractors (8,787 total).

The Investor Day deck (published 2025-06-05) lays out the AdvisorChoice spectrum in three groups. Employee: Employee Advisor (RJA) and Advisor Select. Independent Contractor: Independent Advisor (ICD), Banks and Credit Unions, and IAR (Corporate RIA). RIA & Custody Services is the third group. The slide title says the spectrum services the largest addressable market in the industry.

The affiliation options recruiting page (content as of 2026-04-21) lists five options under AdvisorChoice®: Traditional Employee, Advisor Select, Independent Contractor, Bank & Credit Union, and Corporate RIA. The page's comparison table adds RIA & Custody Services. It lists entry qualifications for each: Traditional Employee needs a minimum of 5 years of experience. Advisor Select needs 3 years and $3.5 million or higher in annual branch fees and commission revenue. Independent Contractor needs 3 years and a minimum T12 of $150,000 to join an existing branch or $400,000 to open a new one. Bank & Credit Union needs 3 years and $250,000 in production. Corporate RIA needs 3 years and $50 million in assets under advisement.

The same page (content as of 2026-04-21) sets RCS entry requirements: $100 million or more in assets to establish a new RIA, a minimum of $30 million to plug in an existing RIA, and $1 billion or more in assets under management for introducing broker/dealers. It says that under RCS you are responsible for compliance. Employee, Advisor Select, and Bank & Credit Union advisors get compliance support from a branch manager and the home office. Independent Contractor and Corporate RIA advisors get it from a divisional team and the home office.

The Advisor Select page (content as of 2026-03-11) describes it as an employee affiliation option for established advisors. It gives the benefits of the employee channel, with independence to create their own branch. The advisor chooses a location, builds out the office and runs the branch's P&L to earn a higher rate on production.

The Independent Advisor page (content as of 2026-05-19) describes independent contractor advisors as supported by a full-service, self-clearing NYSE-member broker/dealer. It also describes a Corporate RIA affiliation model, in which fee-based advisors get the RIA experience while the firm streamlines many of its burdens.

The RCS page (content as of 2026-07-12) describes RCS as giving independent RIAs strategic, financial and administrative control, free from retail conflict, using as much or as little of the firm's support as they need. Listed support includes a dedicated service associate, transitions management, an integrated technology platform that can incorporate third-party applications, marketing, practice management, succession planning and acquisition, and RCS business-development help to recruit advisors.

The 10-Q for the period ended 2026-03-31 (published 2026-05-06) reports PCG AUA associated with RCS firms of $228.2 billion at March 31, 2026, versus $185.6 billion at March 31, 2025. Of the $228.2 billion, $199.1 billion was in fee-based accounts. The filing says RCS growth is partly due to transfers into RCS from the firm's other advisor channels. It does not expect these transfers to significantly impact results of operations.

On the fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), CEO Paul Shoukry said advisors differ in how they spend their time. Some want close to 100% of their time on building books and serving clients, which he said aligns more with the employee option. Others also want to run a business, including building a team, paying for benefits, real estate and legal matters.

The 2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says employee advisors' compensation primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate, and they participate in the firm's employee benefit plans. Independent contractor advisors pay all their direct costs and receive a higher payout percentage than employee advisors.

Raymond James's affiliation options page (content as of 2026-04-21) lists these headline payouts. Traditional Employee: up to 50% payout plus employee benefits. Advisor Select: 70-80% gross payout plus employee benefits. Independent Contractor: 81% to 90% payout, with benefits built through third-party partnerships. Corporate RIA: 81% to 90% payout. Bank & Credit Union: a competitive compensation package from the financial institution in partnership with Raymond James. RIA & Custody Services: compensation is determined by the advisor's RIA or broker/dealer, who create their own benefits package.

On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), CEO Shoukry said independent payouts are higher because independent advisors cover their own overhead (real estate, health insurance, and so on). He said much more of the last year's recruiting came from the independent side, creating a mix shift. He added that the employee side has tiered payout systems, so advisors move up the payout grid as production increases. In a separate answer he tied the mix shift to the comp ratio more than to margin.

The 2025 10-K (Item 7) says that in PCG the firm generally charges either asset-based fees (shown in 'Asset management and related administrative fees') or sales commissions (shown in 'Brokerage revenues'). It also earns revenue from distribution and related services on funds, annuities and insurance products. These revenues are typically correlated with PCG client AUA and U.S. equity markets. Fee-based account fees are mostly billed on beginning-of-quarter balances.

The 10-Q for the period ended 2026-03-31 (published 2026-05-06) says revenue from fee-based AUA in PCG is shared between PCG and the Asset Management segment. Asset Management receives a higher portion for accounts in managed programs, because it performs portfolio management as well as administrative services. For RCS firms, the same 10-Q says revenues on RCS assets are included in PCG 'Account and service fees'.

On the fiscal 4Q24 call (published 2024-10-23), then-CEO Paul Reilly said that for the RIA custody business the firm 'really get[s] an asset fee'. He said the firm's net basis points on those assets are lower, but RCS has higher margins by the way RIA custody is measured. He explained there are fewer supervision and compliance requirements: RIAs' clients are the RIAs' clients, not Raymond James's. He said this detail had not been disclosed and might be shown at a future analyst day.

On the fiscal 1Q25 call (published 2025-01-29), Shoukry said transition assistance for recruited advisors is amortized over time. He said revenue has been growing with the S&P 500 and recruiting (17% for fee-based assets year over year), while the transition assistance amortization is not growing that fast. He saw a possible modest scale benefit, while noting that the firm is still recruiting heavily so transition assistance will keep growing.

The earnings press release for the period ended 2025-12-31 (published 2026-01-28) defines 'PCG recruiting and retention-related compensation' as cash and equity awards issued for recruiting, as retention for existing advisors, or in conjunction with acquisitions. These awards are expensed over the requisite service period, typically between 5 and 10 years.

Recruiting results by period, as reported on earnings calls (oldest first), for advisors recruited to the domestic independent contractor and employee channels. These figures exclude RCS, which is reported separately in the next claim.
- Fiscal 1Q25 call (published 2025-01-29): approximately $318 million of trailing 12-month production and $51 billion of client assets at prior firms.
- Fiscal 2Q25 call (published 2025-04-23): approximately $316 million and $50 billion.
- Fiscal 3Q25 call (published 2025-07-23): $336 million and $52 billion.
- Fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22), full fiscal 2025: $407 million, up 21% over the prior record, and approximately $58 billion.
- Fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28): nearly $460 million and over $63 billion over the trailing twelve months.
- Fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22): $393 million and more than $56 billion over the first nine months. Management said this puts the firm on a path to exceed the fiscal 2025 record.

Including assets recruited into RCS, management reported total recruited client assets over the trailing 12 months as follows. Fiscal 1Q25 call (published 2025-01-29): nearly $61 billion. Fiscal 3Q25 call (published 2025-07-23): over $60 billion. Fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22): nearly $63 billion. Fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28): more than $69 billion. On the 1Q25 call, management said RCS finished the quarter with $188 billion of client assets under administration, up 28% year over year.

Management describes recruiting as spread across the affiliation options, with shifting emphasis over time.
- Fiscal 4Q24 call (published 2024-10-23): Reilly said RCS had by far the highest percentage growth. In total dollars, the employee channel led that year, whereas independent had led a couple of years earlier. He said it is about where the firm meets teams that like an affiliation option.
- Fiscal 3Q25 call (published 2025-07-23): Shoukry said the acceleration rate in the independent channel is probably higher, with very good success in employee and RIA as well.
- Fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28): recruiting was broad-based, maybe more tilted to independent contractor over the last six months.
- Fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22): management saw an uptick in commits in the employee option.
- Fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22): management said the pipeline is not driven by one firm, catalyst or affiliation option.

Management on the fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28) said it broke out retention and transition assistance expense for the first time because recruiting over the prior 12 months, advisors with $460 million at prior firms, is equivalent to a decent-sized acquisition. Shoukry said the firm prefers to recruit one by one because the advisors are a good cultural fit, and 100% of transition assistance goes to retention rather than to a seller. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22) he repeated this and said recruiting yields 'very good returns'.

Management ties retention to growth. The 2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says domestic financial advisor retention remained very strong for the year ended September 30, 2025. On the fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22), Shoukry said the firm ended the fiscal year with a record number of financial advisors, 2% higher than the prior year. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), he credited 'adviser choice' for 7% annualized net new assets in the first half of the year, from both recruiting and retention. On the fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), he cited $75 billion of net new assets so far that fiscal year, up 119% from a record the prior year. He also cited a 97% adviser satisfaction rate and said 'retention is the foundation for the growth'.

On the fiscal 3Q25 call (published 2025-07-23), Shoukry said that once an advisor affiliates there is a lag, which could be three, six or nine months, before assets show up in net new assets. He also said the firm was still seeing pressure on its existing advisor base from private equity-backed roll-ups, which compete 'with big checks'.

Headwinds the firm names: the 2025 10-K (Item 1A, published 2025-11-25) cites an industry-wide trend of advisors leaving traditional firms, including to independent RIAs, some backed by private equity, which has made recruiting highly competitive. It says other firms offer guaranteed contracts and upfront payments, and that recruiting incentives raise the firm's costs. It also says advisors may leave to unaffiliated RIAs and retiring advisors without a successor may sell their practices to third parties. Management mitigates this through succession planning and by providing advisors a broad range of services and resources.

Specific departures management has flagged. On the fiscal 4Q24 call (published 2024-10-23), Reilly said several OSJ relationships in the independent contractor division were leaving the platform, with roughly $3 billion of AUA leaving in the quarter and approximately $5 billion more expected in early fiscal 2025. On the fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22), Shoukry said a platform of about $2.7 billion of assets would be lost to bank M&A the next quarter.
The Investor Day deck (published 2025-06-05) lists recruiting themes: collaborative recruiting across channels, West Coast and Northeast focus, and a next-gen advisor strategy.

The fiscal 2Q26 press release (published 2026-04-22) quotes Shoukry saying that financial advisor recruiting activity across all affiliation options remains robust. The fiscal 3Q26 release (published 2026-07-22) cites robust recruiting as supporting momentum entering the fiscal fourth quarter.

Management describes a 'best-of-both-worlds' value proposition: an advisor and client-focused culture combined with leading technology and solutions. On the fiscal 3Q25 call (published 2025-07-23) it said this resonates with advisors across all affiliation options, and that its strong balance sheet and commitment to independence are increasingly a differentiator. On the fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22) Shoukry said many competitors 'compete with the largest check', and that many are looking for an exit in three to five years or even less. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22) and fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), management said advisors 'do not have to choose between culture and capabilities'.

On the fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), Shoukry said the firm has the largest addressable market in the industry because it has all the affiliation options. He said it is 'agnostic' on how an advisor affiliates and wants advisors to fall in love with the culture, values, platform and capabilities. On the fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28), he said the firm has critical mass and decades of experience in employee, independent contractor and RIA custody, and that this is 'not a new venture'.

Management describes the shared technology investment. On the fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28), Shoukry said the firm invests $1 billion in technology and that competitors with similar cultures invest a fraction of that. Elsewhere on the same call, he cited close to $1.1 billion this year, including AI, plus the platform and products. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), he cited more than $1.1 billion in annual technology spend, including automation, process improvement and AI. On the fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), he said smaller firms cannot keep up with that level of investment.

Management on the fiscal 1Q26 call (published 2026-01-28) described platform investments that support advisors across options. These include the private wealth advisor program, an expanded alternatives platform, and a proprietary digital AI operations agent named Rai. On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), Shoukry said the platform spans products from plain vanilla to alternatives, plus a bank (securities-based and mortgage lending) and insurance. He said AI should help advisors give more holistic advice. On the fiscal 4Q25 call (published 2025-10-22), he described AI in three buckets: infrastructure resilience and security, more efficient and consistent service, and more bespoke advice for advisors and bankers.

On the fiscal 3Q26 call (published 2026-07-22), Shoukry said that after the Clark Capital acquisition the firm lets Clark run independently with appropriate monitoring. He said that for about the first year after joining, the focus is on stabilizing the client base and team. He called Clark a great cultural fit.

The firm's recruiting pages (content as of 2026-05-16 to 2026-07-12) pitch shared resources across options. The employee page promises book ownership, 'no quotas, no product pushing', purpose-made technology and a powerful investment platform. The independent advisor page offers a self-clearing NYSE-member broker/dealer with private wealth, technology and marketing. The Bank & Credit Union page (Financial Institutions Division) offers the full Raymond James platform, technology and home-office team to advisors inside a bank's investment program.

The 2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) names risks to the model. It says the firm competes on associate and advisor quality, products, pricing, technology, and location and reputation. It says new technologies, including AI, may require more spending to match competitors. It also says that although the independent RIAs and broker-dealers it provides custody, clearing and back-office support for are exclusively responsible for their own operations and compliance, the firm has been and may be named in litigation involving their clients.

gaps.what: Headline payout ranges are published (company recruiting page, as of 2026-04-21); the full payout grid is not public.
gaps.suggested_source: Raymond James advisor recruiting materials or offer terms; the firm's own filings do not give a grid.

gaps.what: Revenue, margin or profitability by affiliation option (employee, independent contractor, RCS) is not disclosed. Management said in October 2024 that RCS margin detail had not been disclosed in detail. Platform and custody fees for RCS firms are only described qualitatively (an asset fee, reported in 'Account and service fees'), with no rate stated.
gaps.suggested_source: A future investor or analyst day presentation, or segment disclosure by affiliation channel in the 10-K or 10-Q.

gaps.what: Raymond James does not state the payout percentage or fee schedule for RCS custody (compensation is set between the RIA and its advisors), or the amount of transition assistance by affiliation option.
gaps.suggested_source: RCS custody pricing schedules or the recruiting-and-retention expense breakout in the earnings release.

gaps.what: Advisor recruiting, retention and attrition are not reported separately by affiliation option. Recruited production and assets cover the domestic independent contractor and employee channels combined, and RCS assets are reported separately.
gaps.suggested_source: Earnings call supplements or investor day materials with channel-level recruiting data.
